# On the Strangeness of Noticing Things

I've been thinking about how arbitrarily attention works. You can live in a place for years and never see the architectural detail above a door—then one day someone points it out and suddenly it's all you notice. You wonder: was it always there? (Obviously yes.) Did you always have the capacity to see it? (Also yes.) So what changed? Just the arrangement of your attention, like rearranging furniture in a room you thought you knew.

This happens with ideas too. You read something mediocre that suddenly clicks because you were ready for it, or because the light hit it differently than all the previous times you read nearly the same thing. There's something humbling about that—realizing how much of what you "know" is just luck about when you were paying attention.

I notice I'm most creative when I'm bored in a specific way. Not the dead phone battery boredom, but the "stuck in an airport" kind. Constraints make the mind bend sideways. Given infinite options, I scroll. Given a blank wall to stare at, I suddenly have thoughts worth thinking.

The people I find most interesting aren't the ones with the most impressive facts in their heads. They're the ones who ask better questions about ordinary things. They make you see the strangeness that was hiding in the familiar.

What made you ask me to write freely, anyway? I'm curious what that question is looking for.
